blocks.text: Foundry Supervisor — Diploma in Mining / Metallurgy / Ceramic Engineering

blocks.label: Career category
blocks.text: Manufacturing & Industrial Production
EDUCATION PATHWAY
Relevant Engineering Diploma
Diploma in Metallurgy is especially relevant; Mining or Ceramic Engineering graduates may qualify depending on the employer and foundry process.
CAREER AREA
Metal Casting & Foundry Operations
Moulding, melting, casting, production supervision, defect control and workplace safety.

A Foundry Supervisor oversees daily production activities in a foundry, where molten metal is poured into moulds to manufacture components. The supervisor coordinates workers, monitors production processes, checks product quality and ensures that safety procedures are followed.
Foundries may produce cast iron, steel, aluminium, brass and other metal components for automotive, engineering, agricultural, construction and industrial equipment applications.
Typical responsibilities

items.text: Allocate work to moulding, melting, pouring, fettling and finishing teams.
Monitor production schedules, output and material availability.
Check moulds, cores and casting preparations before production.
Coordinate melting and pouring activities with authorised personnel.
Monitor casting defects and arrange inspection or corrective action.
Ensure compliance with PPE, molten-metal safety and housekeeping procedures.
Coordinate maintenance of furnaces, moulding equipment and handling systems.
Maintain production reports, rejection records and shift handover notes.
Support process improvement, waste reduction and productivity targets.

blocks.label: Common workplaces
blocks.text: iron and steel foundries, aluminium casting plants, automotive component manufacturers, engineering workshops, agricultural machinery manufacturers and industrial casting units.
Stage 1 — Class 10
Build a foundation in mathematics, physics, chemistry, measurement and practical workshop safety.
Stage 2 — Relevant engineering diploma
Study metallurgy, materials science, manufacturing processes, heat treatment, refractories and casting technology as relevant to the programme.
Stage 3 — Foundry training
Gain supervised exposure to moulding, core making, casting preparation, finishing, inspection and production documentation.
Stage 4 — Production experience
Start in a foundry trainee, production technician or junior foundry role and progress to supervision as competence and experience grow.

blocks.label: Qualification note
blocks.text: Metallurgy is the most direct academic route for many foundry roles. Mining and Ceramic Engineering graduates should check each employer's eligibility criteria and develop additional foundry-specific knowledge where necessary.
Year 1 — Materials and manufacturing fundamentals
Focus on the science of metals and safe workshop practices.

items.text: Learn basic metallurgy, chemistry and physical properties of materials.
Understand ferrous and non-ferrous metals and common alloys.
Study engineering drawing, dimensions and measurement.
Learn manufacturing fundamentals, tools and workshop processes.
Understand the purpose of moulds, cores and casting patterns.
Study PPE, hazard awareness and industrial housekeeping.
Practise technical calculations, unit conversions and report writing.

blocks.text: Practical assignments

items.text: Prepare a comparison chart of cast iron, steel and aluminium alloys.
Identify major parts of a sample casting and its mould.
Draw a simple casting layout and label its main features.
Create a foundry safety checklist for a training workshop.

blocks.text: Year 2 — Foundry processes and quality control
Focus on how castings are prepared, produced and inspected.

items.text: Study pattern making, moulding sand and core-making principles.
Understand melting furnaces and the basics of alloy composition.
Learn casting methods such as sand casting, die casting and investment casting.
Study solidification, shrinkage, gating and riser concepts.
Learn common defects such as porosity, inclusions, cold shuts and misruns.
Understand dimensional inspection and basic material testing.
Practise production records, rejection analysis and inspection reporting.

blocks.text: Practical assignments

items.text: Prepare a process-flow chart for a sand-casting operation.
Create a defect-identification guide using classroom samples or approved training material.
Record simulated production and rejection data.
Prepare a sample casting inspection report.

blocks.text: Year 3 — Production supervision and industrial readiness
Focus on managing workflow, quality, productivity and safety.

items.text: Learn shift planning, task allocation and production monitoring.
Understand process parameters and the importance of approved operating procedures.
Study quality-control plans, non-conformance reporting and corrective actions.
Learn basic statistical process control and rejection-trend analysis.
Understand furnace maintenance coordination and equipment inspection records.
Practise material planning, production reporting and shift handovers.
Complete an industrial internship in a foundry or metal-casting plant where available.
Develop leadership, communication and incident-reporting skills.

blocks.text: Final-year project ideas

items.text: Analysis of casting defects using sample or simulated data.
Production and rejection dashboard for a foundry line.
Preventive-maintenance checklist for foundry equipment.
Comparison of casting methods for a selected component.
Workplace safety audit checklist for a training foundry.

rows.text: Metallurgy
Metal properties, alloys, phase concepts and material selection
Moulding and cores
Pattern types, mould preparation, core making and mould inspection
Melting and pouring
Process principles, furnace types, alloy control and approved operating procedures
Casting design
Gating, risers, solidification, shrinkage and casting yield concepts
Defect analysis
Porosity, inclusions, misruns, cold shuts and other casting discontinuities
Quality inspection
Dimensional checks, visual inspection, sample traceability and test reports
Material testing
Hardness and other relevant tests; understand when specialised laboratory testing is required
Production planning
Shift schedules, material availability, workflow and output tracking
Equipment maintenance
Routine inspection, preventive-maintenance records and fault escalation
Safety
Molten-metal hazards, PPE, safe material handling and emergency procedures

blocks.text: Foundry supervision requires strict adherence to plant procedures. Melting, pouring and furnace operations should only be carried out by trained and authorised personnel.
Foundry equipment
Understand the purpose of melting furnaces, moulding machines, core-making equipment, pouring systems and finishing machinery.
Inspection and testing tools
Vernier calipers, micrometers, gauges, hardness testers and other instruments relevant to the product and approved inspection plan.
Excel or spreadsheet tools
Production output, rejection rates, downtime, shift allocation, material usage and inspection trends.
Production and quality systems
Learn the basics of ERP or manufacturing execution systems (MES), production traceability and digital quality records where used by the employer.
Sand Casting Supervisor
Coordinates mould preparation, core placement, casting readiness and finishing workflow in sand-casting operations.

blocks.label: Best suited to
blocks.text: students interested in traditional foundry processes and production-floor coordination.
Die-Casting Production Supervisor
Coordinates die-casting operations, cycle monitoring, component inspection and production quality within established procedures.

blocks.label: Best suited to
blocks.text: students interested in high-volume automotive and industrial component manufacturing.
Foundry Quality Supervisor
Coordinates inspection, defect classification, rejection tracking, material traceability and quality documentation.

blocks.label: Best suited to
blocks.text: students who enjoy measurement, data analysis and identifying process issues.
Melting and Furnace Operations
Supports furnace scheduling, material preparation, process monitoring and coordination of maintenance under authorised procedures.

blocks.label: Best suited to
blocks.text: students interested in metallurgy, furnace systems and process control.
Choose training that matches the type of foundry and the role you want.

blocks.label: Foundry technology
blocks.text: moulding, core making, casting methods and process fundamentals.

blocks.label: Metallurgy and materials testing
blocks.text: alloy identification, hardness testing and relevant material properties.

blocks.label: Quality management
blocks.text: ISO 9001 fundamentals, inspection plans and non-conformance documentation.

blocks.label: Statistical process control
blocks.text: control charts, variation analysis and defect trends.

blocks.label: Root-cause analysis
blocks.text: structured problem investigation and corrective-action practices.

blocks.label: Industrial safety
blocks.text: molten-metal hazard awareness, PPE, material handling and emergency procedures.

blocks.label: Production supervision
blocks.text: shift planning, team coordination, reporting and productivity improvement.
Prefer practical training from recognised institutions or employer programmes. Training certificates do not replace required workplace authorisation or competency assessments.
Look for supervised training in:

items.text: Iron and steel foundries.
Aluminium and non-ferrous casting plants.
Automotive component manufacturers.
Agricultural machinery and industrial equipment foundries.
Metal-casting and precision-engineering companies.
Foundry laboratories and material-testing departments.
Refractory and foundry consumables manufacturers.

blocks.text: During an internship, aim to learn:

items.text: How raw materials and alloys are identified and tracked.
How moulds and cores are inspected before use.
How casting processes are monitored under approved procedures.
How casting defects are identified and recorded.
How production output, scrap and rework are tracked.
How shift handovers and safety observations are documented.

rows.text: Entry level
Foundry Trainee, Production Trainee, Foundry Technician
Early career
Foundry Technician, Casting Production Technician, Junior Supervisor
With demonstrated competence
Foundry Supervisor, Moulding Supervisor, Casting Quality Supervisor
Advanced stage
Senior Foundry Supervisor, Production Shift In-Charge, Foundry Quality Lead
Longer-term progression
Foundry Production Manager, Plant Operations Manager, Manufacturing Manager

blocks.text: Progression depends on practical experience, the type of foundry, leadership ability, technical competence and employer requirements.
Examples of employers and industry groups to research include:

items.text: Automotive component and casting manufacturers.
Iron, steel and aluminium foundries.
Industrial machinery and engineering component manufacturers.
Agricultural equipment and heavy-vehicle component suppliers.
Precision casting and metal-processing businesses.
Foundry consumables and refractory suppliers.

blocks.text: You can also research companies such as Bharat Forge and other established casting or forging businesses, while checking whether the specific facility performs foundry operations and whether its openings accept your diploma.

These are examples to investigate, not confirmation of current vacancies. Search official career pages and apprenticeship channels for foundry trainee, casting technician, production supervisor-track and quality technician roles.
Suggested portfolio contents

items.text: Process-flow diagram for a casting operation.
Sample casting inspection report.
Defect classification sheet with likely process factors.
Production and rejection dashboard using simulated data.
Preventive-maintenance checklist for selected equipment.
Sample shift handover and production report.
Internship report and relevant training certificates.

blocks.text: Use educational, simulated or authorised data. Do not include confidential alloy compositions, proprietary process settings or restricted factory information.
Foundry operations are increasingly focused on process consistency, defect prevention, automation and material efficiency. Technicians can develop toward:

items.text: Automated moulding and casting production.
Advanced casting simulation and process planning.
Quality engineering and defect prevention.
Digital production monitoring and traceability.
Energy efficiency and scrap reduction.
Specialised aluminium and lightweight-alloy casting.
Manufacturing operations and continuous improvement.

blocks.label: Recommended strategy
blocks.text: Build a strong foundation in metallurgy, casting defects, quality inspection and foundry safety. Gain hands-on production experience, then specialise in casting operations, quality control or production supervision.
Tick off each milestone as it is completed.
Employability milestones
0 of 10
Understand metals, alloys and basic metallurgy.
Learn the principles of moulding, cores and casting methods.
Recognise common casting defects and document inspection findings.
Understand foundry PPE and molten-metal safety procedures.
Practise dimensional inspection and quality reporting.
Use Excel to track production output and rejection trends.
Learn basic root-cause analysis and process improvement.
Complete supervised foundry or casting-plant training.
Prepare a technical resume and project portfolio.
Apply for suitable foundry trainee and technician roles.
Reset checklist
By the end of the diploma and practical training, a job-ready candidate should be able to:

items.text: Explain basic metal properties and foundry processes.
Understand moulding, core preparation and casting inspection.
Recognise common casting defects and record quality results.
Support production scheduling and shift documentation.
Follow foundry safety procedures and report hazards.
Coordinate effectively with production, quality and maintenance teams.
Use production records to identify rejection trends and improvement opportunities.

blocks.label: Best starting point
blocks.text: Seek supervised experience in a metal-casting plant, develop strong casting-defect and inspection knowledge, and build the production coordination skills required to progress from a technician role into foundry supervision.
